title: Chapter 135 – The Warden's Veil
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Shen Yuhang]

Shen Yuhang draws his sword every morning at the hour of the tiger, and every morning the Garden banner is higher.

He sees it from the practice terrace of the Hall of Weights, a slab of gray flagstones on the north face of Cloud Peak, with a low wall and a long view down the mountain. It is a plain banner, a square of blue linen on a pole, with a small white character sewn in the center: Lin. It flies over the Gate stair. It flew there first on the day the Council made the Garden a Seat, and every year since, some official has found a reason to raise the pole a few feet. This spring it is thirty feet above the stair. Next spring it will be forty.

He cuts the air in front of him. A clean low arc, left to right. His blade is a long narrow Cloud Peak sword with a plain steel hilt, and it makes the soft sound he has loved since childhood, the sound of a thing being parted with great care. He cuts again. The mist of the early morning curls off the blade in two neat halves.

"Your wrist is stiff," says a voice behind him.

He does not turn. "My wrist is fifty-six years old."

"Then you should use a younger one." Wuping comes out onto the terrace in his dark winter robe, a lean careful man gone gray and sallow, with a cup of tea in each hand. He holds one out. "Drink. You have been out here since the fourth watch."

"I am not cold."

"I did not say you were." The Head of Cloud Peak sets the second cup on the wall and leans beside it, studying the banner. "Thirty feet this year."

"I noticed."

"They will want a tower."

"They will have a tower." Shen sheathes his sword. His movements are very precise. He has been precise all his life. "It is the way of things. A banner goes up, and a tower goes up under it, and a gate goes up under that. In another twenty years the Garden will be the Sect, and Cloud Peak a pleasant view."

"That is a gloomy thought."

"It is arithmetic."

Wuping sips his tea. His eyes are shrewd, tired, a little sad. "Yuhang," he says. "I have a thing to tell you, and I would rather you heard it from me."

Shen waits.

"The vacancy in the Hall of Weights is filled. I have given the second chair to Cheng Yun's pupil." A pause. "She is thirty-one. She is a Foundation Late. She is very good."

The mist drifts. A crow lands on the wall, looks at them both, and flies off again.

"I see," says Shen.

"It is not a slight."

"No." His voice is perfectly level. "I am only fifty-six, with a Peak Foundation and a house name that has not produced a Core in forty years. I have served this Hall since I was sixteen. It is not a slight at all."

* * *

The new second chair is waiting for him in the Hall of Weights, behind a desk that was his, and she stands when he enters.

Her name is Lu Fei. She is thirty-one, as Wuping said, slight and square-shouldered, with a plain intelligent face and ink on her fingers. She wears the dark green of the Hall. She has Cheng Yun's way of holding her head a little to one side, as though listening for a small wrong note, and when she bows to Shen her bow is exactly correct and exactly cold.

"Director," she says. "I have taken the liberty of moving your papers."

"To where?"

"The east cabinet. Third shelf." She indicates it. "I did not read them."

"I would not expect you to."

"I would have," says Lu Fei calmly. "But I thought it improper." She pauses. "I wish to say that I did not seek this post. I was told that you had declined it."

"I did not decline it."

"Then someone has misinformed us both." She holds his gaze. She is not afraid of him, which is rare. "I intend to be a good second, Director. I intend to learn from you. I only ask that you do not make me regret it."

He opens his mouth to answer, and finds that he has nothing to say. She is competent. She is honest. She is, in every respect, exactly what the Hall needs, and she has taken his place with a clean bow and an apology, and there is nothing in her he can hate.

It is the most infuriating thing that has happened to him all year.

That night, at the Shen house, he finds the old man asleep with his mouth open, and a bowl of untouched broth on the chair. He sits for a time with his hands on his knees, watching the thin chest rise and fall. A cat sits on the window ledge among the dead peonies. The moon is thin. He thinks, absurdly, of the stone post on the cliff, and the beetle on its side, and how small a thing it was to be afraid of.

"Uncle," he says, very quietly. "What would you do?"

The old man sleeps on. In the garden, a leaf comes down, and lies on the dark earth, and is still.

"I will see you tomorrow," he says, and goes out onto the terrace, and cuts the air until his shoulder burns.

* * *

His uncle is dying, and he has been dying for nine years.

Shen Yuxian lies in a narrow bed in the east room of the Shen house, a square old villa at the foot of Cloud Peak, with a window that looks onto a garden of dead peonies. He was once a Golden Core cultivator, the last in the family. He had a sword like a stroke of lightning. He taught Shen how to hold it. He is eighty-eight years old now and he weighs less than a child, and his Core, which once burned in his belly like a small gold sun, has dimmed to a dull ember, guttering in a draft.

"You are early," says Yuxian. His voice is a thread.

"I could not sleep."

"You never could." The old man's eyes are sunken, but there is a light in them. "Sit. Tell me what has happened."

Shen sits. He tells it plainly, the banner and the chair and the girl. He does not complain. He has never complained. He tells it as he might report a campaign, and when he has finished the old man says nothing for a long while, and the garden outside is very still.

"They have taken everything," says Shen. "The Hall. The Treasury. The Gate. They sit in the Elders' chamber and they argue about grain. A farmer's son holds the stair. A farmer's daughter holds a Seat. And I am a fifty-six-year-old man with a good sword and nothing to put in front of it."

"You have your life."

"I have a house that is ending."

"Ah." Yuxian smiles faintly. "That is the trouble. You think the house is the thing."

"What else would it be?"

"The people in it." The old man closes his eyes. "I have been lying here nine years, Yuhang. I have had time to think. I was a Core cultivator at forty. I thought I had won. And then I climbed the ridge-house stair with that boy, and saw twenty-eight people lying on jade, and a Sect Head with a scarred brow, asleep, and I understood that I had spent forty years being strong for the wrong thing."

"What thing?"

"A name." His breath rasps. "The Shen name. The Core. The Peak. It is a very small thing to be strong for. It dies with you. There is nothing in it."

"I do not understand."

"No," says Yuxian. "You are not meant to. That is what makes you dangerous." His eyes open, and for a moment they are terribly clear. "Listen to me. Whatever they offer you, whatever they say, take no seat from them."

"From whom?"

"You will know." His fingers close, weakly, on Shen's sleeve. "Promise."

Shen looks at the thin hand. He has known that hand all his life. It once held a sword steady for an hour at the edge of a cliff in a gale.

"I promise," he says.

He means it. That is the worst part.

* * *

He remembers the cliff.

He was fourteen, and it was the winter after his father died. Yuxian had taken him up the north face of Cloud Peak at dawn, in a gale, along a ledge no wider than a plank, with a drop on one side that went down into a white roaring cloud. At the end of the ledge, on a shelf of rock, stood a stone post. Yuxian drew his sword and set the point against the top of the post and held it there, perfectly steady, while the wind tore at his robe.

"Hold it," he said.

Shen took the hilt. His arms shook. The blade trembled. The post, which was no bigger than a man's wrist, seemed to dance under the tip.

"I cannot."

"Then you will fall."

"I cannot do it, uncle."

"You are doing it." Yuxian stood close, his hand light on Shen's shoulder. "Look at the post. Not the drop. Not the wind. The post. It is the only thing in the world that is not moving. Everything else is a rumor."

Shen looked. The post was gray, rough, flecked with mica. A tiny beetle was walking up its side. The blade steadied, and steadied, and was still.

"There," said Yuxian. "You see? A sword is not a thing you swing. It is a thing you hold. Hold it long enough, and the world will arrange itself around it."

Forty-two years ago. He has held the sword every day since, and the world has not arranged itself. It has gone on moving, as it always did: in banners and chairs and the slow rising tide of other people's lives. And he has stood in the middle of it, rigid, with the point against the post, waiting.

He wonders, for the first time, what he is waiting for.

* * *

The clerk comes on the third night.

Shen is at his desk in the Hall of Weights, long after the lamps have been snuffed, going through a stack of reports he does not need to read. He does not hear the door. He looks up and the man is simply there, standing on the other side of the desk, in the soft gray tunic of a Registry clerk, with a plum-colored seal on his collar and a cloth satchel in his hand. He is perhaps fifty. He has a long tired face and a neat gray beard. He looks like a man who has been a minor official all his life and is quietly proud of it.

Shen's hand is on his sword before the clerk has finished bowing.

"Peace," says the clerk. "I carry no weapon. I would not be so foolish."

"The Registry is dissolved."

"The House has withdrawn. That is different." The clerk's smile is faint. "I am Third Clerk Pei An. I served the Keeper for twenty-two years. Now I serve the Roll, which has no Keeper, which is a condition my colleagues and I find very trying." He sets the satchel on the desk. "May I sit?"

"No."

"As you wish." He remains standing. "Director Shen, I will be brief. The House is awake. Not the old one, not the Numbers. A new thing, a council of clerks, the Second House if you like. We keep the books. We keep the Chain. We keep the Roll, in the absence of its Keeper, and the Roll, I regret to say, has named a man who is not here." He taps the satchel. "We are in need of a Warden."

"A Warden of what?"

"Of the Roll. A Warden holds the veil in the Keeper's absence. It is an old office, almost forgotten. The last one died in year three-forty. The Warden speaks for the House. The Warden commands the Chain, and the clerks, and what is left of the Numbers." The soft voice does not change. "And the Warden is given, upon taking the veil, a gift."

"What gift?"

The clerk opens the satchel. Inside, wrapped in plum silk, lies a small jade box. He sets it on the desk and lifts the lid.

Shen forgets to breathe.

It is a pill. It is the size of a hen's egg, and it is gold, truly gold, a deep rich living gold that seems to move in the lamplight like honey. It hums. He can feel it from across the desk, a low steady warmth, a kind of promise, in the place beneath the breastbone where his own Qi sits like a small hard stone. He has never seen one. He has read of them. He knows what it is.

"A Core pill," he says. His voice is not steady.

"A Golden Core pill. Level four, high grade." The clerk closes the lid very gently. "The only one the House has left. It was meant for the Keeper. It will serve a Warden as well."

"Why me?"

"Because you are the best sword in Cloud Peak, and the most underestimated." The clerk smiles. "And because you have, I think, a grievance."

* * *

He does not accept that night. He sends the clerk away, and sits for hours with the lamp out and the jade box in front of him, which the clerk has left on the desk.

He has made a promise. He keeps it in his mind like a stone in his shoe. Take no seat from them. But the box is warm, and the room is cold, and at the fourth watch he finds that he has opened the lid and is looking at the pill with the dull compulsion of a man gazing into a well.

It is the Core. It is the thing he has wanted since he was twelve. It is the end of the long gray road, the beginning of three hundred years, the sword at last in a hand that cannot be refused. He has watched the Garden's banner climb thirty feet, and he has watched the girl in the second chair, and he has watched an old man die by inches in a room full of dead peonies. He has been patient. He has been good. He has done everything he was told.

At dawn, he does a thing he has not done in thirty years.

He goes to the Garden.

* * *

It is not what he expected.

He had pictured something grander. Walls, perhaps, or a keep. Instead the Seat sprawls along the hillside in a cheerful mess of whitewashed houses and tiled roofs and washing-lines, with smoke rising from a hundred chimneys, and a smell of wood-smoke and baking. Children run in the lane. Somewhere a refiner's hammer rings. At the arched gate, a small woman of forty-five in a plain gray robe is standing with a ledger under one arm and a little girl clinging to her skirt, and she watches him come up the road without alarm.

"Director Shen," she says. "You are early."

"Head Lin."

"Yue, please." She bows. "I was told you might come."

"By whom?"

"The doors." She smiles slightly. "It is a long story. Will you come in?"

He should say no. He has come only to look. But the girl at her skirt is peering up at his sword with round dark eyes, and the morning is bright, and he finds himself walking through the arch like a man stepping into a river.

She shows him everything. The school. The clinic. The mill. A row of small neat gardens, each fenced with a different color of wattle. She does not hurry. She tells him the names of the children, one by one, and the ages of the grandmothers, and which of the old men is deaf. At the kitchen door a short woman in an apron, with an iron-gray braid and a wooden spoon, looks up from a vast black pot and says, "He's thin," without further comment, and ladles a bowl of porridge into his hands.

He eats it standing. It is hot and good.

"Mother cannot taste it," says Yue, quietly. "She burned the last three pots. Nobody has the heart to tell her."

"I will not say a word."

"Thank you."

In the yard behind the Hall, under a lean-to roof, a gray-haired man in a patched cloak is mending a plow. He glances up as they come. His face is lined and weathered and very still. A small gray animal sits on a barrel beside him, watching Shen with calm dark eyes.

Shen's hand goes, by old reflex, to his sword.

"Don't," says Lin Jian.

It is said quite gently. He does not rise. He sets down the awl, wipes his hands on his knee, and looks at Shen across fifteen paces of trampled earth. He is fifty-one, Shen knows, and looks sixty. There is nothing about him that suggests Purple Mansion. He might be a tinker at a market.

"I have not come to fight," says Shen.

"No."

"I have come to look."

"Of course." Jian nods slowly. "And what have you seen?"

"A farm." The words come out harder than he means. "A farm with a banner."

"Yes."

"You are very proud of it."

"I am very frightened for it," says Jian. "That is not the same." He stands, and now Shen sees how tall he is, how spare, how the shoulders carry a weight that has nothing to do with the plow. "You have a grievance. I know. I have been aware of it since I was twenty-one. I did not mean to give it to you. I was a boy, and you were in my way."

"You took my name in front of the whole Sect."

"I took my own." He spreads his hands. "I would give you whatever I have, Director. A seat. A dinner. A pill, if I could print it. I do not have a Core. I have a hammer and a very old ledger and a family I would die for. If there is anything in this Garden that would ease your road, it is yours."

Shen stares at him.

It is the offer he has wanted for thirty years. It is generous, plain, entirely sincere. And he feels, rising in him like bile, a rage so enormous and so sudden that it frightens him.

He pities me.

"Keep it," he says. "I want nothing from the farm."

"Yuhang—"

"Do not use my name."

He turns on his heel. At the arch he hears the girl's voice calling after him, high and bright, "Good-bye, mister!", and does not look back.

* * *

The clerk is waiting in the Hall of Weights, in the dark, when he returns.

He has not moved. He stands by the desk, with his hands folded in his sleeves, as though he had never left. The jade box is open on the blotter. The pill glows.

"You have been to the Garden," says Pei An.

"Yes."

"And?"

Shen stands in the doorway. He is shaking. There is a pulse in his temple like a drum.

"What does the veil cost?" he says.

"A name."

"Whose?"

"Yours." The clerk's voice is mild. "It is the old rule. A Warden gives up the name he was born with, that he may carry the name of the office. You will forget it slowly. Over a year, perhaps two. By the end you will not hear it in dreams." His eyes are sad. "I will not lie. It is a terrible thing to lose. It is what we all lose. But the veil is a great thing to gain."

"And the Garden?" Shen says. He does not know why he asks.

"The Garden will be well treated." The clerk inclines his head. "The Second House has no quarrel with it. We are not conquerors. We are clerks. Our only interest is that the Roll be kept, the Chain be held, and the eighth Operator be brought safely home when his work is done." He pauses. "You will find that we are not as the old House was. We are much more patient."

Shen thinks of Yuxian, small in the bed. Take no seat from them.

He thinks of the banner, thirty feet high.

He thinks of the pity in a gray man's voice, patient and gentle, offering him a bowl of porridge.

"Do it," he says.

"You are certain?"

"I am certain." His voice cracks. "I have been certain all my life. I am tired of being the only man in the room who is."

The clerk bows.

He takes a scroll from his sleeve. It is a small thing, plum-colored, tied with a cord. He unrolls it on the desk, beside the pill, and from his satchel he takes a brush and a stick of black ink. He writes. He writes a name, slowly, in the oldest script, one stroke at a time, and Shen watches it appear on the paper with a sick dull wonder.

Shen Yuhang.

It is the strangest thing he has ever seen. He has read it a thousand times. It has never looked so small.

"Swallow the pill," says Pei An, "when I touch the flame."

He lifts a candle. The paper catches.

It burns clean and fast, with a cold green light, and a smell like old rain. As the first letters curl, Shen feels it: a pulling, a thinning, as though a long thread were being drawn out of the center of him. He opens his mouth. The gold pill is on his tongue, burning, vast, splitting his skull with light. He hears the clerk's dry voice, very far away, saying good, good, and his own heart pounding, and under it all, quite distinct, a faint small sound like a bell ringing in an empty house.

It is his name, leaving.

* * *

He wakes in the ridge-house.

He does not remember being carried there. He lies on a bed of green jade in a long cold hall, beneath a vault of dark stone, with a veil of plum-colored gauze across his face. There is a hum in the room, low and steady, like the breathing of many sleepers. On either side of him, in long rows, thirty-one still figures lie on jade, their chests rising and falling in perfect unison.

His own chest rises with them.

He sits up. His hands are steady. There is a heat in his belly like a small sun, and when he closes his eyes he can feel the whole Chain, thirty-one threads of breath, shining in the dark like beads on a string. At the head of the hall, on a dais, lies a man in a green robe with a scarred brow, who has slept for fifty-seven years. He can feel the Sect Head breathing. He can feel him dreaming.

Pei An is waiting at the foot of the bed.

"Warden," he says, and bows low.

"What is my name?"

He did not mean to ask. It comes out in a whisper. The clerk lifts his head, and his tired face is full of pity.

"You are the Warden of the Roll."

"That is not a name."

"No." The clerk's voice is gentle. "It is the only one you have."

Shen Yuhang, who was once a man with a sword and a family and an uncle dying in a room of peonies, opens his mouth to answer. He knows there was a word. He knows it had three syllables, and that it began with a sound like a breath. He reaches for it. He reaches again.

Nothing.

He sits for a long time with his hand over his mouth, and the thirty-one sleepers breathe around him, and in the dark of the ridge-house, a Golden Core opens like an eye.
